title: Lamp, Bread, and the Holy Name
summary: God commands pure olive oil for the lamps that burn continually in the tabernacle and twelve loaves set out on the gold table every Sabbath. Then a man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father blasphemes God's name during a fight. After Moses seeks the LORD's ruling, the man is stoned outside the camp, and God gives laws on blasphemy, murder, and injury, including eye for eye and tooth for tooth, applied equally to native and foreigner.
story: Chapter 23 set out the holy calendar. Chapter 24 begins with two things that happen continually inside the tabernacle, the lamps and the bread, before turning abruptly to a story. Apart from the ordination of the priests and the death of Nadab and Abihu (chapters 8 to 10), this is the only story in Leviticus, and like the death of Nadab and Abihu it concerns the danger of treating God's holiness lightly. The story shows the laws of the Holiness Code being applied in a real case in the camp. It belongs with several episodes in the Torah where Moses waits for a ruling from God on a question the law had not yet settled: the unclean men at Passover (Numbers 9), the Sabbath-breaker (Numbers 15), and the daughters of Zelophehad (Numbers 27).
historical:
The golden lampstand and the table for the bread were described in Exodus 25 and made in Exodus 37. The priests kept the lamps burning through the night and replaced the bread every Sabbath. The practice continued for centuries. In 1 Samuel 21 the priest at Nob gave David and his men the consecrated bread that had just been replaced, and the Arch of Titus in Rome, built after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, still shows soldiers carrying away the temple's lampstand. Traditional readers date these laws to Moses at Sinai, while many critical scholars see the Holiness Code in its final form as coming from the late monarchy or the exile.

The law of retaliation, often called by its Latin name lex talionis, appears also in Exodus 21:23-25 and Deuteronomy 19:21. Older Mesopotamian law used the same principle. The Code of Hammurabi, from the eighteenth century BC, required an eye for an eye when a nobleman blinded another nobleman, but only a payment of silver when the victim was a commoner or a slave. Leviticus 24 insists on a single standard for everyone, foreigner and native alike (verse 22). Later Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, understood the law to require monetary compensation equal to the injury rather than literal maiming, and many scholars think it served that way in practice.
cultural:
Olive oil was the main source of light in the ancient world, burned in small clay lamps in every house. The finest oil came from olives beaten or pressed by hand rather than crushed in a press, and that is what the sanctuary received. The lamps shining through the night and the bread always on the table pictured a household where the host is always present. The twelve loaves stood for the twelve tribes, set before God continually as a sign of the covenant (verse 8), and then eaten by the priests.

In the ancient world a name was more than a label. It stood for the person's character, reputation, and presence. To curse God's name was to attack God himself, and in Israel, where God was king, it was a form of treason. The man in this story had an Egyptian father, and the text raises, without saying so, the question of whether Israel's laws applied to someone of mixed descent. The answer is yes: the law applies to the foreign resident and the native alike. Those who heard the curse laid their hands on the man's head, most likely declaring that the guilt of the words they had heard rested on him and not on them. Later Jewish interpretation, reading verse 16 with its verb that can mean to pronounce or designate, held that the offense required actually pronouncing the divine name, and the Jewish custom of not speaking God's personal name aloud was reinforced by this passage. Jews often refer to God simply as the Name.
literary: The chapter joins two very different kinds of text: ritual instructions (verses 1 to 9) and a narrative with laws embedded in it (verses 10 to 23). The word continually (verses 2, 3, 4, and 8) ties the first part together. The second part is carefully shaped. Many scholars have noted that verses 13 to 23 form a chiasm, a mirrored pattern: the command to stone the blasphemer (verses 13 and 14) matches the carrying out of the sentence (verse 23); the law on blasphemy (verses 15 and 16) matches the one-law-for-all principle (verse 22); killing a person and killing an animal (verses 17 and 18) are repeated in reverse (verse 21); and at the center stands "fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (verse 20). The structure puts equal justice at the heart of the passage.

outline.t: Oil for the lamps that burn continually
The twelve loaves on the gold table
Life for life, eye for eye: one law for all

doctrines.note: God's name stands for God himself. To curse it is not a lapse of manners but an assault on the one who rescued and rules Israel. The chapter treats reverence for God's name as foundational to the community's life.

The law of retaliation limits punishment to what fits the offense and applies the same standard to every person, native or foreign. It rules out both leniency for the powerful and excessive vengeance for the wronged.
The twelve loaves are set out every Sabbath "as a permanent covenant" (verse 8). The bread before God's presence was a standing sign that all twelve tribes belonged to him and lived by his provision.

words.note: Tamid, continually or regularly. It describes the lamps that never go out and the bread that is always on the table. The same word names the daily burnt offering of morning and evening. It speaks of faithful, unbroken service before God, not a one-time act.

Shem, name. In verses 11 and 16 the text refers to God's name simply as the Name, a usage that became common in later Judaism. God's name is his revealed identity; to know it is to know him, and to curse it is to reject him.

Naqav, a verb whose basic meaning is to pierce or mark, and which can also mean to designate or pronounce. The BSB renders it as blaspheme (verses 11 and 16). Whether it refers to cursing or to pronouncing God's name disrespectfully was debated by later interpreters and shaped Jewish reverence for the divine name.

Tachat, instead of or in place of. It is the small word in "life for life", "eye for eye", and "tooth for tooth". It expresses equivalence: what is given must correspond to what was taken. The principle limits revenge as much as it requires justice.

christ: Jesus addressed verse 20 directly in the Sermon on the Mount: "You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you not to resist an evil person" (Matthew 5:38-39). He did not abolish justice but called his followers, as individuals, to give up the right to personal revenge. When his disciples were criticized for picking grain on the Sabbath, he pointed to David eating "the consecrated bread, which was lawful only for the priests" (Mark 2:26). Jesus called himself "the light of the world" (John 8:12) and "the bread of life" (John 6:35), which readers have connected with the lamp and bread of this chapter, though those sayings are rooted more directly in other feasts and in the manna. Most strikingly, Jesus himself was condemned for blasphemy (Mark 14:64) and put to death outside the city, and Stephen, the first Christian martyr, was stoned outside Jerusalem on the same charge, praying for those who killed him (Acts 7:58-60).

hard.q: Why was a man stoned to death for cursing God during a fight?
hard.a: The penalty seems out of all proportion to many modern readers, and the text does not soften it. In Israel's setting, God was the nation's king and his name was bound up with his presence among them, so cursing it was a kind of treason against the covenant on which the community's life depended. The case was not decided in anger: the man was held in custody until Moses received God's ruling, those who heard him bore witness, and the law applied equally to native and foreigner. Jewish tradition later narrowed the offense to pronouncing the divine name in a curse and surrounded capital cases with strict safeguards. Christians have generally held that this penalty belonged to Israel's civil law under God's direct rule and is not a model for the church or for modern states. The New Testament adds a painful irony: Jesus and Stephen were both executed on charges of blasphemy they did not commit, and neither responded with a curse. The chapter still leaves readers with the seriousness of how God's name is treated.

questions: The lamps burned continually and the bread was always before God. What practices in your life are steady and daily rather than occasional?
The law of retaliation limited punishment to what fit the offense. When you have been wronged, how do you resist the urge to make the other person pay more than they owe?
The blasphemer's words came out in a fight. How does anger reveal what we really think of God or of others?
